name.text: Matatu routes: when do the two fares become equal?

questiontext.text:

generalfeedback.text:
What the graph shows. Each line gives the fare (vertical axis, in KSh) for a trip of a given length (horizontal axis, in km). Each grid line across is {@ys@} shillings and each grid line up is {@xs@} km. A point on a line is a trip together with its fare on that route. The point where the two lines cross is the one trip that costs the same on both routes.

  1. Find the point where the blue line (Route A) and the dashed red line (Route B) cross.
  2. From that point go straight down to the horizontal (distance) axis and read the value: {@dstar@} km.
  3. From the same point go straight across to the vertical (fare) axis: the fare is KSh {@cstar@}. The question asks for the distance, so the answer is the value read on the horizontal axis.

Check using the cost functions. At 0 km the lines start at KSh {@fA@} (Route A) and KSh {@fB@} (Route B). The rate (the gradient) is the extra fare for each km, which we find from the start and the crossing point: Route A: \( \dfrac{ {@cstar@} - {@fA@} }{ {@dstar@} } = {@rA@} \) KSh per km; Route B: \( \dfrac{ {@cstar@} - {@fB@} }{ {@dstar@} } = {@rB@} \) KSh per km. So

\[ \text{Route A: } C = {@fA@} + {@rA@}d \qquad \text{Route B: } C = {@fB@} + {@rB@}d. \]

The fares are equal when the two expressions are equal:

\[ {#sgl#} \;\Longrightarrow\; {@rA-rB@}d = {@fB-fA@}\;\Longrightarrow\; d = {@dstar@}\text{ km}, \]

and then \( C = {@fA@} + {@rA@}\times {@dstar@} = {@cstar@} \) and \( C = {@fB@} + {@rB@}\times {@dstar@} = {@cstar@} \), the same fare on both routes. ✓

Answer (a): {@dstar@} km. Common mistake: giving {@cstar@}, the fare, instead of the distance.

(b) What the value in (a) means. The crossing point is where the two fares are equal, but it is also where the cheaper route changes. Graph 2 shades the two sides of the crossing:

  • To the left of the crossing (trips shorter than {@dstar@} km) the line of {#nameS#} is lower, so {#nameS#} is the cheaper route. It starts at the lower fare (KSh {@fS@} against KSh {@fL@}), so it wins on short trips.
  • At the crossing ({@dstar@} km) both routes charge KSh {@cstar@}.
  • To the right of the crossing (trips longer than {@dstar@} km) the line of {#nameL#} is lower, so {#nameL#} is the cheaper route. {#nameS#} adds {@rS@} KSh for every extra km but {#nameL#} adds only {@rL@}, so the starting advantage of {#nameS#} is used up by the crossing and then reversed. The green arrows show the fares getting further apart on each side.

Answer (b): both routes charge the same fare, KSh {@cstar@}, for a {@dstar@} km trip; for shorter trips {#nameS#} is cheaper and for longer trips {#nameL#} is cheaper.

Why the other explanations are wrong.

  • The same wording with the two routes swapped: the lines show that {#nameS#}, not {#nameL#}, is lower on the left of the crossing.
  • One route cheaper for every trip: the lines cross, so the lower line changes at {@dstar@} km. A route that is cheaper on both sides would need the lines to touch without crossing, but these lines have different gradients, so they cross.
  • The two numbers the wrong way round: the horizontal axis is distance and the vertical axis is fare, so the crossing is {@dstar@} km and KSh {@cstar@}, not KSh {@dstar@} and {@cstar@} km.
  • The same rate per km after {@dstar@} km: the rates are the gradients, {@rA@} and {@rB@} KSh per km, and they do not change along a straight line. It is the total fares, not the rates, that are equal at the crossing.
